newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's military to fight for ecological image.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's military to fight for ecological image.

text.p: Brazil's military is heading for duty in the Amazon, Gen. Alberto Cardoso, the president's liaison with the military, said late on Wednesday.

The general, who is not related to President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, said military objectives in the Amazon would be to preserve the environment and support police in battling "armed gangs," a new and growing threat to national security.

Telling foreign journalists a new National Defence Policy announced last week would redirect resources to the rain forest in the north, he made clear the aim was not to involve the armed forces in direct conflict with criminals, which is the constitutional duty of the Federal Police, Brazil's equivalent to the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation.

Hypothetically, he said, Brasilia might use the military in operations like last month's eviction of freelance gold miners from the huge Serra Leste gold deposit in the northern state of Para, where some 300 soldiers formed a "ring of steel" while Federal Police rounded up the "garimpeiros."
"Our doctrine is that this sort of sideline work of police action involving the Armed Forces will only take place if we are certain the possibility of conflict is very low," he said.

With antagonism between Argentina and Brazil laid to rest by the success of the Mercosur customs union, he said it was time to confront new enemies -- arms and drugs smugglers and a "false opinion" abroad about Brazil's ecological zeal.

"The possibility of conflict in the south is of a very low probability," said Cardoso, the top military officer in the presidential palace. "The Amazon, on the other hand, is an immense space only sparsely populated. Such a big empty area must have a Brazilian presence."

In addition, he said there was an awareness of the need for "caution" over critical reports from environmental pressure groups that projected a "false and unreal opinion" internationally about Brazil. "The concern is with our image. We are not destroyers of the Amazon; we preserve Indians; we have a zeal for the environment," Cardoso said.

The new policy stresses Brazil's defensive posture while it extends the definition of threats to territorial integrity to include organised crime and armed gangs in unnamed neighbouring countries as well as environmental vandalism.
